title: Lamrim: karma
hook: actions have results; small actions can grow large

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lamrim's stair on death. Your line was certain, uncertain: it will come, and nobody knows when. Did you make the call or say the word you'd been putting off? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

Drip. A leaky tap over an empty bucket in the corner of a shed. Drip. Nobody notices one drop. It's too small to matter. Drip. Come back in a week, and the bucket is full to the rim, maybe spilling over onto the floor. No single drop did it. All of them did. The Dhammapada uses almost exactly that picture, a water pot filled drop by drop, and the lamrim takes it up as its next stair. If death is certain and its time unknown, the obvious question is: then what does what I do today actually add up to?
screen: `DRIP: ONE DROP, TOO SMALL TO MATTER.` → `A WEEK LATER, A FULL BUCKET.` → `WHAT DOES TODAY ADD UP TO?`

segments.voice: First, actions have results. Karma, in Buddhist teaching, means intentional action: what you do, say and think on purpose. The lamrim teaches that such actions bring results in kind. Kind actions tend toward happiness, harmful ones toward suffering. Not as a reward or a punishment handed down by anyone, but the way a seed becomes the plant it is. Second, small grows large. The Dhammapada warns against thinking lightly of a harm, saying it won't come back to me, because a water pot fills from falling drops. The next verse says the same of good: no one should think lightly of it either, because the wise fill up with good, gathered little by little. The lamrim adds a picture of its own: a tiny seed can become a huge tree. A small act, repeated or left to ripen, can become very large. Third, two companions to that idea. You don't meet the results of what you never did. And what you did do doesn't simply vanish because time passed. Together, these make the teaching very practical: nothing small is wasted, in either direction. Fourth, why this follows death on the staircase. If life is precious and its end unknown, a person might despair of ever doing anything big enough. Karma answers: you don't have to. A held tongue, a shared lunch, a minute of patience in traffic, each one is a drop. Buckets are made of drops. So are habits, and in this teaching, so are lives.
screen: `ACTIONS HAVE RESULTS, LIKE SEEDS.` · `A POT FILLED DROP BY DROP.` · `NOTHING SMALL IS WASTED.` · `BUCKETS ARE MADE OF DROPS.` · then, large: `SMALL GROWS LARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one small good deed. For now, sit and let the breath settle. Then choose the deed. Make it small enough that it will actually happen today: a thank-you text, holding a door, putting away something someone else left out. Picture yourself doing it, simply. Then picture it as one drop going into a bucket, quiet, unremarkable, and real. Rest there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Lamrim, the next stair: karma. Intentional actions bring results in kind, and small actions can grow large. Today's word.
Your line: small grows large. Today, do the small good deed you chose, and don't wait for it to feel important. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: In lamrim practice, students reflect on how intentional actions bring results in kind and how small actions grow, then try to take care with small harms and small kindnesses in daily life.

fork.setup: you're about to skip a small kindness because it seems too small to matter. what does today's stair say?
options: skip it: only big deeds count.
do it: small actions grow, and nothing small is wasted.
save it up for one big deed later.
fork.reveal: the Dhammapada's water pot and the lamrim's seed say the same thing: small grows large, in both directions.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is cosmic payback.
what it means: intentional actions bring results in kind, and small ones can grow large.
what a scholar hears: the lamrim stage on karma, using the image of a seed growing into a tree and echoing Dhammapada 121 and 122.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 121 (small harms fill the pot drop by drop)

the stage on karma: results in kind, karma grows, unmet if not done, not lost
sources.work: Tsongkhapa, Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path (Lamrim Chenmo)

notes: Dhammapada 121 and 122 are paraphrased, not quoted; confirm the verse numbers and the paraphrase (the wise filling with good, little by little).
The lamrim's general features of karma (certain in kind, growing, not met if not done, not lost once done) are given without a count; confirm phrasing.
The seed-to-huge-tree image is a common lamrim illustration; confirm it is fair to attribute to 'the lamrim' generally.
'Not as a reward or a punishment handed down by anyone' describes the Buddhist account of karma; a Keeper may want to phrase it more carefully.
